title: The Blue Whale
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived. An adult can reach thirty metres in length, longer than three buses parked in a row, and weigh up to one hundred and fifty tonnes, which is more than twenty-five elephants. Its heart is the size of a small car, and its tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant. Yet this giant feeds on some of the smallest animals in the sea. Hunted almost to extinction in the twentieth century, the blue whale is now slowly recovering. This passage describes how it lives, feeds and communicates, and how people are trying to save it.

Blue whales belong to a group called baleen whales. Instead of teeth, they have long plates of a hornlike material called baleen hanging from the upper jaw, which work like a giant comb. The whale takes a huge mouthful of water, which may contain krill, small shrimp-like animals about the length of a finger. It then pushes the water out through the baleen with its tongue, leaving the krill trapped inside to be swallowed. At the peak of the feeding season, a blue whale can eat around four tonnes of krill a day, and it may swallow forty million of them.

The whales feed mainly in cold, rich waters near the poles in summer, where krill are abundant. In winter, many migrate to warmer seas near the equator, to give birth. A calf is born tail first after a pregnancy of about eleven months, and it is already about seven metres long and weighs around two tonnes. It drinks several hundred litres of its mother's milk a day, which is so rich in fat that the baby gains about ninety kilograms every day. After about six months the calf is weaned, by which time it has more than doubled in length.

Like all whales, blue whales are mammals, not fish. They are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and feed them with milk, and they breathe air through lungs. When a whale surfaces, it blows out a spout of warm, moist air through two blowholes on the top of its head. The spout of a blue whale can rise nine metres into the air, and it can be seen from a great distance. A whale can stay underwater for twenty minutes or more, and dives to depths of around two hundred metres to find food, although it usually stays closer to the surface.

Blue whales are among the loudest animals on the planet. They produce low-frequency moans, groans and pulses, which can reach 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine at close range. The sounds are so low that they are partly below the range of human hearing, and they can travel for hundreds of kilometres through the water. Scientists believe that whales use these calls to find one another across the vast ocean, and males may also use them to attract mates. Recently, researchers have noticed that the pitch of the calls of blue whales in many parts of the world has been slowly falling, and nobody is sure why.

In the early twentieth century, whalers armed with explosive harpoons and fast steam-powered ships hunted blue whales in huge numbers. As many as 350,000 were killed in the Southern Ocean alone, and by the 1960s, the population had fallen to a few thousand. An international ban on hunting blue whales was introduced in 1966, and numbers have since recovered slowly. Today, there are thought to be between ten and twenty-five thousand blue whales in the world, but this is a small fraction of the original population. Whales breed slowly, producing a single calf every two or three years, so recovery will take many decades.

Today the threats are different. Ships sometimes collide with whales, particularly in busy shipping lanes, and noise from engines and sonar may interfere with their calls. Whales can become tangled in fishing nets, and the warming of the oceans may reduce the supply of krill. Dr Ana Reyes, a marine biologist who studies whales from small boats, says that simple measures can help: ships can slow down in areas where whales are common, and shipping lanes can be moved. She believes that the recovery of the blue whale will be one of the great success stories of conservation, provided that people continue to protect it.
